claim: Mechanoelectrical transduction is a cellular signalling pathway where physical stimuli are converted into electro-chemical signals by mechanically activated ion channels.
source: Mechanoelectrical transduction is a cellular signalling pathway where physical stimuli are converted into electro-chemical signals by mechanically activated ion channels.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the abstract that draws from established scientific understanding of mechanoelectrical transduction.

claim: Melanoma cells exhibit mechanically activated currents that are dependent on TMEM87a (Elkin1).
source: We describe here the presence of mechanically activated currents in melanoma cells that are dependent on TMEM87a, which we have renamed Elkin1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing MA currents in melanoma cells and their dependence on Elkin1.

claim: Heterologous expression of Elkin1 in PIEZO1-deficient cells is sufficient to reconstitute mechanically activated currents.
source: Heterologous expression of this protein in PIEZO1-deficient cells, that exhibit no baseline mechanosensitivity, is sufficient to reconstitute mechanically activated currents.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing MA currents in HEK-293T P1KO cells expressing Elkin1.

claim: Melanoma cells lacking functional Elkin1 exhibit defective mechanoelectrical transduction.
source: Melanoma cells lacking functional Elkin1 exhibit defective mechanoelectrical transduction, decreased motility and increased dissociation from organotypic spheroids.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Elkin1-KO melanoma cells showing reduced MA currents.

claim: Melanoma cells lacking functional Elkin1 exhibit decreased motility.
source: Melanoma cells lacking functional Elkin1 exhibit defective mechanoelectrical transduction, decreased motility and increased dissociation from organotypic spheroids.
evidence: This is supported by migration assay data showing reduced migration in Elkin1-KO cells.

claim: Melanoma cells lacking functional Elkin1 exhibit increased dissociation from organotypic spheroids.
source: Melanoma cells lacking functional Elkin1 exhibit defective mechanoelectrical transduction, decreased motility and increased dissociation from organotypic spheroids.
evidence: This is supported by spheroid assay data showing more Elkin1-KO cells dissociating from spheroids.

claim: Elkin1 deletion is associated with increased cell-substrate adhesion.
source: By analysing cell adhesion properties, we demonstrate that Elkin1 deletion is associated with increased cell-substrate adhesion and decreased homotypic cell-cell adhesion strength.
evidence: This is supported by AFM data showing increased unbinding force between Elkin1-KO cells and LM511.

claim: Elkin1 deletion is associated with decreased homotypic cell-cell adhesion strength.
source: By analysing cell adhesion properties, we demonstrate that Elkin1 deletion is associated with increased cell-substrate adhesion and decreased homotypic cell-cell adhesion strength.
evidence: This is supported by AFM data showing decreased unbinding force between Elkin1-KO cells.

claim: Elkin1 supports a PIEZO1-independent mechanoelectrical transduction pathway.
source: We therefore conclude that Elkin1 supports a PIEZO1-independent mechanoelectrical transduction pathway and modulates cellular adhesions and regulates melanoma cell migration and cell-cell interactions.
evidence: This is supported by data showing MA currents in PIEZO1-deficient cells expressing Elkin1 and persistence of MA currents in WM266-4 cells after PIEZO1 knockdown.

claim: Elkin1 modulates cellular adhesions and regulates melanoma cell migration and cell-cell interactions.
source: We therefore conclude that Elkin1 supports a PIEZO1-independent mechanoelectrical transduction pathway and modulates cellular adhesions and regulates melanoma cell migration and cell-cell interactions.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental data including migration assays, AFM measurements, and spheroid assays.

claim: The discovery of PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 has highlighted the diverse array of cells and tissues that express ionotropic force sensors.
source: The discovery of the mammalian MA channels, PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 (Coste et al., 2012; Coste et al., 2010), has highlighted the diverse array of cells and tissues that express such ionotropic force sensors (Albuisson et al., 2013; Florez-Paz et al., 2016; Hung et al., 2016; Maksimovic et al., 2014; Martins et al., 2016; Miyamoto et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014; Rocio Servin-Vences et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The activation of PIEZO channels by externally applied mechanical stimuli underpins the senses of touch, proprioception and hearing.
source: The activation of these channels by externally applied mechanical stimuli underpins our senses of touch, proprioception and hearing (Florez-Paz et al., 2016; Maksimovic et al., 2014), and contributes to the physiological function of mechanoresponsive tissues such as the vasculature (Evans et al., 2018; Li et al., 2014), the urothelium (Martins et al., 2016; Miyamoto et al., 2014) and the cartilage (Rocio Servin-Vences et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: PIEZO channels contribute to the physiological function of mechanoresponsive tissues such as the vasculature, the urothelium and the cartilage.
source: The activation of these channels by externally applied mechanical stimuli underpins our senses of touch, proprioception and hearing (Florez-Paz et al., 2016; Maksimovic et al., 2014), and contributes to the physiological function of mechanoresponsive tissues such as the vasculature (Evans et al., 2018; Li et al., 2014), the urothelium (Martins et al., 2016; Miyamoto et al., 2014) and the cartilage (Rocio Servin-Vences et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: PIEZO1 can be activated by cell-generated forces in addition to exogenously applied forces.
source: Recent evidence has suggested that PIEZO1 is not only activated by exogenously applied forces but can also be activated by cell-generated forces (Blumenthal et al., 2014; Ellefsen et al., 2019; Nourse and Pathak, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MA channels may be involved in inside-out mechanical signalling and contribute to the ability of cells to probe the physical nature of their microenvironment.
source: Thus, MA channels may be involved in inside-out mechanical signalling and contribute to the ability of cells to probe the physical nature of their microenvironment.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from the cited evidence about PIEZO1 activation by cell-generated forces.

claim: PIEZO channels do not account for all mammalian MA channel activity.
source: Because PIEZO channels do not account for all mammalian MA channel activity, identifying additional MA channels and characterising their function represent important outstanding challenges in the field (Dubin et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Inside-out mechanical signalling has been implicated in the development and metastasis of cancers.
source: Inside-out mechanical signalling has been implicated in the development and metastasis of cancers.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the subsequent citations about mechanical changes in cancer.

claim: The stiffening of the local microenvironment has been shown to impact tumourigenicity or invasiveness.
source: The stiffening of the local microenvironment (Kai et al., 2016), changes in cell packing and cell-cell adhesions (Cichon et al., 2015) and the tumour topology (Lee et al., 2016a) have all been shown to impact tumourigenicity or invasiveness.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Changes in cell packing and cell-cell adhesions have been shown to impact tumourigenicity or invasiveness.
source: The stiffening of the local microenvironment (Kai et al., 2016), changes in cell packing and cell-cell adhesions (Cichon et al., 2015) and the tumour topology (Lee et al., 2016a) have all been shown to impact tumourigenicity or invasiveness.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The tumour topology has been shown to impact tumourigenicity or invasiveness.
source: The stiffening of the local microenvironment (Kai et al., 2016), changes in cell packing and cell-cell adhesions (Cichon et al., 2015) and the tumour topology (Lee et al., 2016a) have all been shown to impact tumourigenicity or invasiveness.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Melanoma cancer progression/transformation is directly linked to mechanical changes at a cellular level.
source: In the case of melanoma, cancer progression/transformation is directly linked to mechanical changes at a cellular level: cells become more compliant (Jonas et al., 2011), exhibit increased contractility (Paszek et al., 2005; Sanz-Moreno et al., 2011) and display altered morphology during transformation (Poole and Müller, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Melanoma cells become more compliant during cancer progression/transformation.
source: In the case of melanoma, cancer progression/transformation is directly linked to mechanical changes at a cellular level: cells become more compliant (Jonas et al., 2011), exhibit increased contractility (Paszek et al., 2005; Sanz-Moreno et al., 2011) and display altered morphology during transformation (Poole and Müller, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Melanoma cells exhibit increased contractility during cancer progression/transformation.
source: In the case of melanoma, cancer progression/transformation is directly linked to mechanical changes at a cellular level: cells become more compliant (Jonas et al., 2011), exhibit increased contractility (Paszek et al., 2005; Sanz-Moreno et al., 2011) and display altered morphology during transformation (Poole and Müller, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Melanoma cells display altered morphology during transformation.
source: In the case of melanoma, cancer progression/transformation is directly linked to mechanical changes at a cellular level: cells become more compliant (Jonas et al., 2011), exhibit increased contractility (Paszek et al., 2005; Sanz-Moreno et al., 2011) and display altered morphology during transformation (Poole and Müller, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: During metastasis, cells must break away from the primary tumour and navigate microenvironments with diverse physical properties.
source: During the process of metastasis, cells must break away from the primary tumour and navigate microenvironments with diverse physical properties including: confined pores in the ECM, the planar interface of the basement membrane, or tracks and channels formed from ECM fibres or the earlier passage of cancerous cells (Wolf et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature and represents established knowledge about metastasis.

claim: Deflection-activated currents were measured in all WM266-4 cells tested (10/10).
source: Deflection-activated currents were measured in all WM266-4 cells (10/10) and the current amplitude increased with increasing stimulus size (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data from pillar array experiments.

claim: The current amplitude of deflection-activated currents increased with increasing stimulus size in WM266-4 cells.
source: Deflection-activated currents were measured in all WM266-4 cells (10/10) and the current amplitude increased with increasing stimulus size (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The reversal potential of deflection-activated currents in WM266-4 cells was +6.6 mV.
source: The reversal potential, as determined from a current-voltage relationship for the peak MA current, was +6.6 mV, indicating that the underlying current was passed by a non-selective cation channel (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The reversal potential of +6.6 mV indicates that the underlying current was passed by a non-selective cation channel.
source: The reversal potential, as determined from a current-voltage relationship for the peak MA current, was +6.6 mV, indicating that the underlying current was passed by a non-selective cation channel (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured reversal potential and established knowledge about ion channel biophysics.

claim: Larger deflections were required to activate currents in WM115 cells compared to WM266-4 cells.
source: We additionally tested whether MA currents were activated in WM115 melanoma cells (isolated from the primary tumour from the same patient as WM266-4). Larger deflections were required to activate currents in WM115 cells, compared to WM266-4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: WM115 melanoma cells were isolated from the primary tumour from the same patient as WM266-4.
source: We additionally tested whether MA currents were activated in WM115 melanoma cells (isolated from the primary tumour from the same patient as WM266-4).
evidence: This is a statement about the origin of the cell line, which is established knowledge about these cell lines.

claim: Displacements at the interface between melanoma cells and their substrate evoke MA currents.
source: These data demonstrate that displacements at the interface between melanoma cells and their substrate evoke MA currents.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on pillar deflection experiments.

claim: WM266-4 cells on LM511-coated arrays were more sensitive to pillar deflections than WM266-4 cells on uncoated arrays.
source: WM266-4 cells on LM511-coated arrays were more sensitive to pillar deflections than WM266-4 cells on uncoated arrays (ordinary two-way ANOVA, n = 20 and 10 cells respectively, **p=0.005; Sidak's multiple comparison, *p=0.02).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: LM511 supported the highest degree of transmigration in comparison with other LM isoforms (LM111, LM211, LM411 and EHS-LM).
source: Note, LM511 supported the highest degree of transmigration, in comparison with other LM isoforms, LM111, LM211, LM411 and EHS-LM.
evidence: This is supported by transwell assay data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Half-maximal activation of MA currents in WM266-4 cells on LM511 occurred with approximately 18 nm of substrate deflection.
source: Under these conditions, current saturation occurred within the stimulus range, allowing us to use a Boltzmann sigmoidal fit to determine the MA current sensitivity. Half-maximal activation of MA currents was seen with approximately 18 nm of substrate deflection (Effective deflection ED50; standard error = 20.5 nm).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and curve fitting analysis.

claim: There is a correlation between migratory properties and MA current sensitivity to deflections applied at cell-substrate contact points.
source: These data indicate a correlation between migratory properties and the MA current sensitivity to deflections applied at cell-substrate contact points.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that LM511, which promotes migration, also increases MA current sensitivity.

claim: The biophysical characteristics of the observed deflection-activated currents are consistent with those previously described for PIEZO1.
source: PIEZO1 is an obvious candidate for mediating this activity, in particular because the biophysical characteristics of the observed deflection-activated currents are consistent with those previously described for this channel (Poole et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with published data on PIEZO1.

claim: In PIEZO1 knock-down WM266-4 cells cultured on LM511-coated pillar arrays, MA currents were activated in response to pillar deflection in 10/10 cells measured.
source: In PIEZO1 knock-down cells cultured on LM511-coated pillar arrays, MA currents were activated in response to pillar deflection in 10/10 cells measured and the resulting stimulus-response curves were similar to controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The stimulus-response curves in PIEZO1 knock-down WM266-4 cells were similar to controls.
source: In PIEZO1 knock-down cells cultured on LM511-coated pillar arrays, MA currents were activated in response to pillar deflection in 10/10 cells measured and the resulting stimulus-response curves were similar to controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Treatment with Ruthenium Red did not inhibit MA currents in WM266-4 cells.
source: Similarly, treatment with Ruthenium Red (RR, a channel blocker that inhibits PIEZO1 and TRP channels) did not inhibit these MA currents (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: PIEZO1 is unlikely to be the MA channel responsible for the current measured in WM266-4 cells.
source: From these data we conclude that PIEZO1 is unlikely to be the MA channel responsible for the current measured in WM266-4 cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PIEZO1 knockdown and Ruthenium Red experiments.

claim: Two known non-selective cation channels were identified in the WM266-4 proteome: PIEZO1 and TRPV2.
source: Two known non-selective cation channels were identified, PIEZO1 and TRPV2.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic analysis data.

claim: Ruthenium Red is a channel blocker of both PIEZO1 and TRPV2.
source: However, RR is a channel blocker of both PIEZO1 (Coste et al., 2012) and TRPV2 (Caterina et al., 1999), indicating that neither likely mediates the deflection-evoked currents in WM266-4 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Neither PIEZO1 nor TRPV2 likely mediates the deflection-evoked currents in WM266-4 cells.
source: However, RR is a channel blocker of both PIEZO1 (Coste et al., 2012) and TRPV2 (Caterina et al., 1999), indicating that neither likely mediates the deflection-evoked currents in WM266-4 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of inhibition by Ruthenium Red.

claim: Elkin1 is expressed in melanoma cells but not healthy melanocytes.
source: We prioritised the investigation of Elkin1 due to its expression in melanoma cells but not healthy melanocytes, its expression in additional mechanosensitive cells (Alveolar Type II cells) and its upregulation in additional human cancers (Human Protein Atlas [Uhlén et al., 2005] available from www.proteinatlas.org).
evidence: This is supported by data from the Human Protein Atlas.

claim: Elkin1 is expressed in Alveolar Type II cells.
source: We prioritised the investigation of Elkin1 due to its expression in melanoma cells but not healthy melanocytes, its expression in additional mechanosensitive cells (Alveolar Type II cells) and its upregulation in additional human cancers (Human Protein Atlas [Uhlén et al., 2005] available from www.proteinatlas.org).
evidence: This is supported by data from the Human Protein Atlas.

claim: Elkin1 is upregulated in additional human cancers.
source: We prioritised the investigation of Elkin1 due to its expression in melanoma cells but not healthy melanocytes, its expression in additional mechanosensitive cells (Alveolar Type II cells) and its upregulation in additional human cancers (Human Protein Atlas [Uhlén et al., 2005] available from www.proteinatlas.org).
evidence: This is supported by data from the Human Protein Atlas.

claim: Knockdown of Elkin1 transcript resulted in a dramatic reduction in MA currents to deflections up to 1000 nm.
source: We generated miRNA constructs targeting Elkin1 and found that knockdown of Elkin1 transcript resulted in a dramatic reduction in MA currents to deflections up to 1000 nm (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Elkin1 contributes to MA currents in melanoma cells.
source: These data suggested that Elkin1 contributes to MA currents in melanoma cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Elkin1 knockdown experiments.

claim: Human Elkin1 isoforms 1 and 3 contain six predicted transmembrane domains.
source: Three human isoforms (representing splice variants) of Elkin1 have been identified: isoforms 1 and 3 (555 and 494 aa respectively), contain six predicted TM domains (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by transmembrane topology prediction shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Human Elkin1 isoform 2 does not contain any predicted transmembrane domains.
source: Isoform 2 (181 aa) does not contain any predicted TM domains and was not examined in this study.
evidence: This is based on transmembrane topology prediction.

claim: Both hsElkin1-iso1 and hsElkin1-iso3 are present at the cell surface.
source: Note, both hsElkin1-isoform1 and hsElkin1-isoform3 are present at the cell surface.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot analysis of biotinylated surface proteins shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Both hsElkin1-iso1 and hsElkin1-iso3 were present at the plasma membrane as well as the intracellular fraction.
source: Both isoforms were present at the plasma membrane, as well as the intracellular fraction.
evidence: This is supported by cell-surface biotinylation and Western blot analysis.

claim: hsElkin1-iso1-GFP localised to both the membrane and a dispersed population of dynamic foci.
source: hsElkin1-iso1-GFP localised to both the membrane and a dispersed population of dynamic foci, while hsElkin1-iso3-GFP assembled into structures that were co-labelled by Lifeact-mCherry. (Figure 2E–J; Figure 2—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy imaging shown in Figure 2E-J.

claim: hsElkin1-iso3-GFP assembled into structures that were co-labelled by Lifeact-mCherry.
source: hsElkin1-iso1-GFP localised to both the membrane and a dispersed population of dynamic foci, while hsElkin1-iso3-GFP assembled into structures that were co-labelled by Lifeact-mCherry. (Figure 2E–J; Figure 2—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy imaging shown in Figure 2E-J.

claim: hsElkin1-iso1-GFP localised to the Golgi apparatus.
source: Laser-scanning confocal imaging to visualise hsElkin1-iso1-GFP throughout the cell revealed that this protein also localised to the Golgi apparatus (as previously described [Hirata et al., 2015﻿]): in contrast, hsElkin1-iso3-GFP was enriched in actin-based ruffles that were present at the cell periphery (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy imaging shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and cited literature.

claim: hsElkin1-iso3-GFP was enriched in actin-based ruffles that were present at the cell periphery.
source: Laser-scanning confocal imaging to visualise hsElkin1-iso1-GFP throughout the cell revealed that this protein also localised to the Golgi apparatus (as previously described [Hirata et al., 2015﻿]): in contrast, hsElkin1-iso3-GFP was enriched in actin-based ruffles that were present at the cell periphery (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy imaging shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: HEK-293T P1KO control cells exhibited no current activation in response to stimuli within the deflection range of 1–1000 nm (0/8 cells).
source: The control cells exhibited no current activation in response to stimuli within our deflection range of 1–1000 nm (0/8 cells).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from pillar array experiments.

claim: Mechanically activated currents were detected in response to pillar deflection in HEK-293T P1KO cells expressing either hsElkin1-iso1 or hsElkin1-iso3 (8/8 and 9/9 respectively).
source: However, mechanically activated currents were detected in response to similar stimuli in HEK-293T P1KO cells expressing either hsElkin1-iso1 or hsElkin1-iso3 (8/8 and 9/9 respectively) (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The observed current kinetics in HEK-293T P1KO cells expressing Elkin1 were consistent with direct mechanical activation.
source: The observed current kinetics were consistent with direct mechanical activation (Figure 3—source data 1) and the mechanically evoked currents measured in WM266-4 cells (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of current kinetics data.

claim: Mechanically evoked currents could be measured in N2a Piezo1-/- cells expressing hsElkin1-iso1 (6/8 cells responding) compared to 4/10 control cells.
source: We confirmed that we could mechanically evoke currents in a second cell line lacking PIEZO1, N2a Piezo1-/- (Moroni et al., 2018), where 6/8 cells expressing hsElkin1-iso1 responded to pillar deflection compared to 4/10 control cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression of Elkin1 is sufficient to confer MA channel activity to substrate deflection and cell indentation stimuli in a heterologous system lacking endogenous PIEZO channels.
source: From these data we conclude that the expression of Elkin1 is sufficient to confer MA channel activity to substrate deflection and cell indentation stimuli in a heterologous system lacking endogenous PIEZO channels, but not to membrane stretch.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the heterologous expression experiments in HEK-293T P1KO and N2a Piezo1-/- cells.

claim: The expression of Elkin1 is not sufficient to confer MA channel activity to membrane stretch.
source: From these data we conclude that the expression of Elkin1 is sufficient to confer MA channel activity to substrate deflection and cell indentation stimuli in a heterologous system lacking endogenous PIEZO channels, but not to membrane stretch.
evidence: This is supported by the lack of currents in response to HSPC stimulation.

claim: MA currents were evoked in HEK-293T P1KO cells expressing either hsElkin1-iso1 (6/6 cells) or hsElkin1-iso3 (5/5 cells) in response to indentation.
source: The HEK-293T P1KO cell line is unresponsive to indentation, (0/6 cells responding) as previously described (Dubin et al., 2017; Figure 3C,D); in contrast, MA currents were evoked in cells expressing either human Elkin1 isoform (hsElkin1-iso1 6/6 cells, hsElkin1-iso3 5/5 cells responding) (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Indentation-evoked currents were only measured in a small fraction of N2a Piezo1-/- cells expressing hsElkin1-iso1 or hsElkin1-iso3 (1/10 and 1/12 responding respectively compared to 0/8 control cells).
source: Indentation-evoked currents were only measured in a small fraction of N2a Piezo1-/- cells expressing hsElkin1-ios1 or hsElkin1-iso3 (1/10 and 1/12 responding respectively compared to 0/8 control cells, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: No currents were evoked by membrane stretch using HSPC in HEK-293T cells overexpressing human Elkin1 (negative pressure: hsElkin1-iso1 0/11, hsElkin1-iso3 0/13, positive pressure: hsElkin1-iso1 0/5, hsElkin1-iso3 0/5 responding).
source: When membrane stretch was applied using high-speed pressure-clamp (HSPC), no currents were evoked in negative controls or HEK-293T cells overexpressing human Elkin1 (negative pressure: hsElkin1-iso1 0/11, hsElkin1-iso3 0/13, positive pressure: hsElkin1-iso1 0/5, hsElkin1-iso3 0/5 responding) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Both positive and negative pressure evoked currents in all positive controls where PIEZO1 was expressed.
source: In contrast, both positive and negative pressure evoked currents in all positive controls where PIEZO1 was expressed (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Mus musculus homolog of Elkin1-iso1 shares 93% sequence identity at the protein level with the human variant.
source: The Mus musculus homolog of Elkin1-iso1 shares 93% sequence identity at the protein level with the human variant.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Robust MA currents were not observed in HEK-293T P1KO cells following expression of mouse mmElkin1-iso1 (5/8 cells responding).
source: However, we did not observe robust MA currents in HEK-293T P1KO cells following expression of mouse mmElkin1-iso1 (5/8 cells responding, Figure 4A,B), indicating a difference in sensitivity between these homologous proteins.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: There is a difference in sensitivity between mouse and human Elkin1 homologs.
source: However, we did not observe robust MA currents in HEK-293T P1KO cells following expression of mouse mmElkin1-iso1 (5/8 cells responding, Figure 4A,B), indicating a difference in sensitivity between these homologous proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the difference in MA current activation between mouse and human Elkin1.

claim: The divergence in amino acid sequences between mouse and human Elkin1 primarily resides in the N-terminus of the proteins.
source: Alignments between the protein sequences (Corpet, 1988) revealed that the divergence in amino acid sequences primarily resides in the N-terminus of the proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expression of N-terminal truncation mutants of hsElkin1 conferred similar MA currents to those of the wild type protein.
source: However, expression of N-terminal truncation mutants of hsElkin1 conferred similar MA currents to those of the wild type (WT) protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that this region is not required for MA currents.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The N-terminal region of hsElkin1 is not required for MA currents.
source: However, expression of N-terminal truncation mutants of hsElkin1 conferred similar MA currents to those of the wild type (WT) protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that this region is not required for MA currents.
evidence: This is an inference based on the truncation mutant data.

claim: Introducing the two human residues (F271L and N292G) into the mouse polypeptide led to robust MA channel activity.
source: Introducing the two human residues into the mouse polypeptide (mmElkin1-iso1-F271L-N292G), led to robust MA channel activity, in contrast with WT mmElkin1-iso1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing mmElkin1-iso1-F271L-N292G to WT mmElkin1-iso1.

claim: Introducing either of the mouse residues (L210F or G231N) into the human polypeptide led to a reduction in the amplitude of the MA currents measured.
source: Conversely, introducing either of the mouse residues into the human polypeptide (hsElkin1-iso3-L210F or hsElkin1-iso3-G231N) led to a reduction in the amplitude of the MA currents measured (Figure 4A,B), despite the fact that these variants were still present in the plasma membrane (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The hsElkin1-iso3-L210F and hsElkin1-iso3-G231N variants were still present in the plasma membrane.
source: Conversely, introducing either of the mouse residues into the human polypeptide (hsElkin1-iso3-L210F or hsElkin1-iso3-G231N) led to a reduction in the amplitude of the MA currents measured (Figure 4A,B), despite the fact that these variants were still present in the plasma membrane (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by cell-surface biotinylation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Two residues (F271L and N292G in mouse, L210F and G231N in human) can account for the differences in activity between the mouse and human Elkin1 proteins.
source: These data indicate that two residues can account for the differences in activity between the mouse and human proteins, and that these two residues are required for the activation of robust Elkin1-dependent currents by substrate deflection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutagenesis experiments.

claim: Two residues (L210 and G231 in human) are required for the activation of robust Elkin1-dependent currents by substrate deflection.
source: These data indicate that two residues can account for the differences in activity between the mouse and human proteins, and that these two residues are required for the activation of robust Elkin1-dependent currents by substrate deflection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutagenesis experiments.

claim: Duplicate clonal populations of wild-type (WT) and Elkin1-knockout (KO) WM266-4 cells were isolated using CRISPR/Cas9.
source: To address this question, we used CRISPR/Cas9 to gene-edit cells such that no functional Elkin1-iso1/3 were expressed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). Duplicate clonal populations of wild-type (WT) and Elkin1-knockout (KO) cells were isolated.
evidence: This is supported by the CRISPR/Cas9 strategy and validation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reduced deflection-activated currents were observed in the Elkin1-KO clones compared to the WT.
source: Using pillar arrays, we observed reduced deflection-activated currents in the Elkin1-KO clones compared to the WT (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: A residual current at large deflections was still present in some Elkin1-KO cells.
source: A residual current at large deflections was still present in some KO cells; we hypothesise that this effect is due to minor compensation from PIEZO1 (Supplementary file 1 and as noted previously [Rocio Servin-Vences et al., 2017]) or the activity of an as-yet-unidentified MA channel.
evidence: This is an observation from the data with a speculative explanation.

claim: Elkin1 is required for sensitive MA channel activity in WM266-4 cells.
source: Nevertheless, these data confirm that Elkin1 is required for sensitive MA channel activity in WM266-4 cells.

claim: WT WM266-4 clones (3B6 and 3E9) were indistinguishable from WT controls in transwell migration assays.
source: While transmigration of the WT clones was not different from control populations, both Elkin1-KO clones exhibited reduced transmigration (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by transwell assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Both Elkin1-KO WM266-4 clones exhibited reduced transmigration compared to controls.
source: While transmigration of the WT clones was not different from control populations, both Elkin1-KO clones exhibited reduced transmigration (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by transwell assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The transmigration phenotype in the Elkin1-KO was rescued by overexpression of hsElkin1-iso3.
source: This phenotype could be rescued by the transient overexpression of wild-type hsElkin1-iso3.
evidence: This is supported by transwell assay data showing rescue of transmigration.

claim: Overexpression of hsElkin1-iso3 L210F did not rescue the transmigration defect in Elkin1-KO cells.

claim: A375 Elkin1-KO cells exhibited reduced transmigration compared to A375 WT cells.
source: The A375 Elkin1-KO cells exhibited reduced transmigration, compared to the A375 WT cells (Figure 5E), indicating that the link between Elkin1 activity and migration is not restricted to WM266-4 cells and can be measured in a cell line where PIEZO1 is functionally active.
evidence: This is supported by transwell assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The link between Elkin1 activity and migration is not restricted to WM266-4 cells and can be measured in a cell line where PIEZO1 is functionally active.
source: The A375 Elkin1-KO cells exhibited reduced transmigration, compared to the A375 WT cells (Figure 5E), indicating that the link between Elkin1 activity and migration is not restricted to WM266-4 cells and can be measured in a cell line where PIEZO1 is functionally active.
evidence: This is an inference based on the A375 data.

claim: Disruption of Elkin1 impairs mechanosensitivity and cell migration.
source: We therefore conclude that disruption of Elkin1 not only impairs mechanosensitivity, but also cell migration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined electrophysiology and migration data.

claim: The Elkin1-KO clones exhibited reduced track mean speed on both LM511 and PLL substrates.
source: The Elkin1-KO clones exhibited reduced track mean speed on both substrates (Figure 6C) and a reduced distance migrated from origin (calculated as the Euclidean distance, Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by 2D migration assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The Elkin1-KO clones exhibited a reduced distance migrated from origin on both LM511 and PLL substrates.
source: The Elkin1-KO clones exhibited reduced track mean speed on both substrates (Figure 6C) and a reduced distance migrated from origin (calculated as the Euclidean distance, Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by 2D migration assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Elkin1 modulates cell migration in unconfined environments.
source: These data demonstrate that Elkin1 modulates cell migration in unconfined environments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the 2D migration assay data.

claim: The mean migration speed was lower in the Elkin1-KO clones compared to WT in confined (quasi-1D) migration.
source: The mean migration speed was lower in the Elkin1-KO clones compared to WT (Figure 6F) (22% reduction in the mean Elkin1-KO track mean speed), indicating that disrupting Elkin1 inhibits the ability of cells to undertake both unconfined and confined migration on hard surfaces.
evidence: This is supported by quasi-1D migration assay data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Disrupting Elkin1 inhibits the ability of cells to undertake both unconfined and confined migration on hard surfaces.
source: The mean migration speed was lower in the Elkin1-KO clones compared to WT (Figure 6F) (22% reduction in the mean Elkin1-KO track mean speed), indicating that disrupting Elkin1 inhibits the ability of cells to undertake both unconfined and confined migration on hard surfaces.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined 2D and quasi-1D migration data.

claim: At every time point (24, 48, and 72 hr), more Elkin1-KO cells had dissociated from the spheroid compared to WT.
source: At every time point, more Elkin1-KO cells had dissociated from the spheroid compared to WT (Figure 7A–G) and at 48 and 72 hr the Elkin1-KO cells were further away from the edge of the spheroid (Figure 7H, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by spheroid assay data shown in Figure 7A-G.

claim: At 48 and 72 hr the Elkin1-KO cells were further away from the edge of the spheroid compared to WT.

evidence: This is supported by spheroid assay data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Elkin1-KO cells dissociated more readily from the spheroid mass during the first 12 hr after spheroid implantation.

evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 7—videos 1 and 2.

claim: In 3D collagen gels, the mean track speed was not different between WT and Elkin1-KO clones.
source: We investigated whether isolated Elkin1-KO cells embedded in 3D collagen gels exhibited a change in migratory properties to determine if an increase in migration speed could account for these data. In this 3D environment, the mean track speed was not different between WT and Elkin1-KO clones, however the track straightness was reduced in the Elkin1-KO clones (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by 3D migration assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: In 3D collagen gels, the track straightness was reduced in the Elkin1-KO clones.
source: We investigated whether isolated Elkin1-KO cells embedded in 3D collagen gels exhibited a change in migratory properties to determine if an increase in migration speed could account for these data. In this 3D environment, the mean track speed was not different between WT and Elkin1-KO clones, however the track straightness was reduced in the Elkin1-KO clones (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by 3D migration assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Elkin1-KO cells were less spherical as they broke away from the spheroid.
source: We additionally noted that the Elkin1-KO cells were less spherical as they broke away from the spheroid (Figure 7I, Figure 7—figure supplement 1) as they were in the 3D collagen gels (Figure 7—figure supplement 2)).
evidence: This is supported by sphericity analysis shown in Figure 7I.

claim: The increased distance of the Elkin1-KO cells from the spheroid is due to facilitated dissociation, not due to increased migration speed.
source: These data thus suggest that the increased distance of the Elkin1-KO cells from the spheroid is due to facilitated dissociation, not due to increased migration speed.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined spheroid and 3D migration data.

claim: The unbinding of LM511 from Elkin1-KO cells required a larger force than the WT clone (37% increase in the mean of the maximum unbinding force).
source: The unbinding of LM511 from Elkin1-KO cells required a larger force than the WT clone (37% increase in the mean of the maximum unbinding force) (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: Lower unbinding force was measured after homotypic contact between Elkin1-KO cells, in comparison with WT cells (27% decrease in the mean of the maximum unbinding force).

evidence: This is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 8C,D.

claim: In chimeric spheroids, Elkin1-KO cells were found in the outer layer of the spheroid and the WT cells in the core.
source: To determine if deletion of Elkin1 influenced cell-cell organisation over longer time scales, we created chimeric spheroids between Elkin1-KO and WT cells by mixing equal numbers of a GFP-labelled and an unlabelled clone. Regardless of which clone expressed the GFP, the spheroid was organised such that Elkin1-KO cells were found in the outer layer of the spheroid and the WT cells in the core (triplicate experiments, 23 spheroids total) (Figure 8E,F).
evidence: This is supported by chimeric spheroid imaging data shown in Figure 8E,F.

claim: In chimeric spheroids, the partitioning of cells was partially rescued in Elkin1-KO cells expressing hsElkin1-iso3 but not hsElkin1-iso3-L210F.
source: To test whether the channel activity of Elkin1 is linked to cell partitioning within spheroids, we stably transfected Elkin1-KO cells with either hsElkin1-iso3 or hsElkin1-iso3-L210F. In chimeric spheroids the partitioning of cells was partially rescued in cells expressing hsElkin1-iso3 but not hsElkin1-iso3-L210F, where cells were evenly distributed throughout the resulting spheroids (duplicate experiments, 6 and 9 spheroids, respectively) (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by chimeric spheroid rescue data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of Elkin1 has a differential effect on cell-substrate versus cell-cell binding.
source: Taken together these data indicate that deletion of Elkin1 has a differential effect on cell-substrate versus cell-cell binding and regulates cell-cell associations in organotypic spheroids.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AFM and spheroid data.

claim: Deletion of Elkin1 regulates cell-cell associations in organotypic spheroids.
source: Taken together these data indicate that deletion of Elkin1 has a differential effect on cell-substrate versus cell-cell binding and regulates cell-cell associations in organotypic spheroids.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spheroid data.

claim: MA ion channel activity was identified at the cell-substrate interface in WM266-4 metastatic melanoma cells using elastomeric pillar arrays.
source: We report the identification of MA ion channel activity at the cell-substrate interface in WM266-4 metastatic melanoma cells, using elastomeric pillar arrays to apply fine mechanical stimuli to cells via their connections to the subjacent matrix (Poole et al., 2014; Sianati et al., 2019), thus simulating deflections arising from cell-generated forces.
evidence: This is supported by the pillar array experimental data and cited methodology.

claim: Elastomeric pillar arrays simulate deflections arising from cell-generated forces.

evidence: This is a statement about the methodology supported by citations.

evidence: This is a comparison based on the measured ED50 value and cited literature.

evidence: This is supported by comparison with cited literature on cell-generated forces.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

evidence: This is based on sequence comparison analysis.

source: There is limited information regarding the physiological function of Elkin1, however the gene is expressed in diverse human tissues including organs where mechanical feedback is important, such as the lungs and the bladder (GTEx portal).

claim: The latency between stimulus and response for Elkin1-dependent currents was <2 ms.
source: The latency between stimulus and response (<2 ms) and the activation time constant (<1 ms) were similar to those reported for PIEZO1-mediated currents (Poole et al., 2014; Rocio Servin-Vences et al., 2017) and sufficiently rapid to suggest that the Elkin1-dependent current is directly activated by the mechanical stimulus (Christensen and Corey, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of current kinetics data.

evidence: This is supported by analysis of current kinetics data.

claim: The latency and activation time constant of Elkin1-dependent currents are sufficiently rapid to suggest that the current is directly activated by the mechanical stimulus.

claim: The mechanical response profile of Elkin1 is distinct from other MA ion channels.

evidence: This is a comparison based on the experimental data and cited literature.

claim: PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 respond to membrane stretch, cell indentation and substrate deflection.
source: This mechanical response profile is distinct to other MA ion channels: PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 respond to membrane stretch, cell indentation and substrate deflection (Coste et al., 2010; Poole et al., 2014; Rocio Servin-Vences et al., 2017) (though PIEZO2 is less sensitive to membrane stretch than PIEZO1 [Wang et al., 2019]) and TRPV4 responds only to substrate deflections in mammalian cells (Rocio Servin-Vences et al., 2017).

evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The process of cell dissociation from a spheroid mass is defined by a complex interplay between the strength of cell-cell adhesions, the contractility of the cells at the edge of the spheroid and the physical characteristics of the surrounding matrix.
source: The process of cell dissociation from a spheroid mass is defined by a complex interplay between the strength of cell-cell adhesions, the contractility of the cells at the edge of the spheroid and the physical characteristics of the surrounding matrix (Ahmadzadeh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Elkin1 expression regulates the balance between cell-cell and cell-matrix adhesion.
source: Our data demonstrate that Elkin1 expression regulates cell-substrate and cell-cell binding forces. In addition, the partitioning of cells within the organotypic spheroids was dependent on Elkin1. We therefore propose that Elkin1-dependent expression regulates the balance between cell-cell and cell-matrix adhesion; ablation of the protein increases invasion of surrounding matrix (by reducing cell-cell adhesions and facilitating cellular dissociation) and slows migration (by increasing cell-substrate binding).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AFM and spheroid data.

claim: Ablation of Elkin1 increases invasion of surrounding matrix by reducing cell-cell adhesions and facilitating cellular dissociation.
source: We therefore propose that Elkin1-dependent expression regulates the balance between cell-cell and cell-matrix adhesion; ablation of the protein increases invasion of surrounding matrix (by reducing cell-cell adhesions and facilitating cellular dissociation) and slows migration (by increasing cell-substrate binding).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data on adhesion and spheroid dissociation.

claim: Ablation of Elkin1 slows migration by increasing cell-substrate binding.

evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data on adhesion and migration.
